Perceiving the universe—which exists within oneself—as being like a city seen in a mirror, appearing as if arisen externally through *māyā*, just as [objects appear] through sleep; so it is said.
Salutations to that venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who at the time of awakening directly realizes his own non-dual Self; salutations to Him in the form of the Śrī Guru. || 1 ||
Like a sprout within a seed, this world was previously devoid of conceptual construction; yet,
like a magician or a great yogi, it is made variegated by the diverse manifestations of space and time fashioned through *māyā*, and is brought forth by his own will.
To that venerable form of the Guru, to Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, let this salutation be offered. || 2 ||
The vibration of which, though of the nature of existence, appears as the object of the unreal;
which the Vedic word "That thou art" directly reveals to those who take refuge in it;
and by the direct realization of which there shall be no further return to the ocean of worldly existence.
To that venerable form of the Guru, to the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti, let this salutation be offered. || 3 ||
But whose knowledge— resplendent with the light of a great lamp situated within a jar full of various apertures— pulsates outward through the doors of the senses such as the eyes;
this entire world shines only by following that very [knowledge] which shines, thinking "I know."
To that embodiment of the venerable Guru, to Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, be this salutation. || 4 ||

Those who argue with great delusion— like women, children, the blind, and the dull-witted— regard the body, the vital breath, the senses, and even the flickering intellect as empty, yet falsely imagine "I" to be them;
[salutations] to Him who destroys the great delusion fashioned by the play of the power of Māyā.
To him, the embodiment of the venerable Guru, to Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, this salutation. || 5 ||

Resembling the sun or moon eclipsed by Rāhu due to being shrouded by Māyā, that person who, through the withdrawal of the instruments of perception, became one consisting of pure existence in deep sleep,
is recognized at the time of awakening by the thought, "I slept previously."
To him, the embodiment of the venerable Guru, to the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti, be this salutation. || 6 ||

To that venerable form of the Guru, to Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, let this salutation be offered. || 7 ||

Deluded by *māyā*, this person perceives the universe through distinctions such as cause and effect, the relationship between master and servant, likewise that between disciple and teacher, and in the form of father and son; whether in dream or in the waking state, he is thus bewildered.
To him, the embodiment of the venerable Guru, to the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti, let this salutation be offered. || 8 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the sun, the moon, and the individual soul— this entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, appears as the eightfold form of Him alone;
for those who investigate, nothing else whatsoever exists apart from that all-pervading Supreme Lord.
To him, the embodiment of the venerable Guru, to Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, let this salutation be offered. || 9 ||
Since this "state of being the self of all" has been clearly established in this hymn, by hearing it, reflecting upon its meaning, meditating on it, and reciting it,
one's own state of lordship— accompanied by the great manifestation of being the self of all— shall arise spontaneously.
Furthermore, this would be accomplished as an eightfold sovereignty that is unimpeded.
Mānasollāsa (The Delight of the Mind)

To him, the embodiment of the venerable Guru, to Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, be this salutation. || 1 ||
May Vināyaka grant me auspiciousness; may Sarasvatī grant me auspiciousness;
may Maheśvara grant me auspiciousness.
May Sadāśiva grant me auspiciousness forever. || 1 ||
The sages know that there is no gain higher than the attainment of the Self;
for the sake of attaining that, the wise one praises his own self as the Supreme Lord. (2)
He who, having entered the universe created by his own will, abides within the mind—that very Supreme Lord is praised by this hymn. (3)
The conventional usage "it exists" and "it shines" proceeds; but upon what object is that existence and that luminosity established? (4)
Is [this] in each of those various objects, or rather in the Lord who is the self of all?
And what is the nature of lordship, the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), and the state of being the self of all? (5)
How may one know the individual soul (jīva), and what is the means for that knowledge?
What would be the fruit of that knowledge, and how might oneness (ekatva) come to be? (6)
"How can the Self be both omniscient and the creator of all? To the disciple who asks this, the teacher begins to speak as follows: (7)
Within this [Self] are these worlds; within it is this entire universe. Yet, through Māyā, it appears as if external, like one's own body reflected in a mirror.
Just as the universe contained within oneself appears as if separate in a dream, so too should this phenomenal world be discerned during the waking state. (9)
It is certain that in a dream, the existence of objects is nothing other than one's own existence;
what distinction, then, exists for those insentient things that perish so rapidly in the waking state? (10)
The manifestation of objects in a dream is not due to anything other than self-luminosity;
the wise determine that it is exactly the same even in the waking state. (11)
Just as one who has awakened does not perceive the objects shown by sleep,
so too, after the arising of perfect knowledge, one no longer perceives the universe.
When the individual soul, sleeping through beginningless illusion, awakens,
it then realizes the non-dual reality, which is without birth, sleep, or dream.
When the awakening to one's own Self occurs through the sacred scriptures, by the grace of the teacher, through the power of yoga practice, and also by the favor of the Lord; || 14 ||

Just as one perceives food eaten and residing in the stomach as being of one's own very nature, so too does the Lord of Yogis perceive the entire universe as swallowed by the fullness of the I-consciousness (pūrṇāhaṃtā). || 15 ||
Just as one who, having become a king in a dream, enjoys pleasures as desired, and having conquered an enemy on the battlefield accompanied by a fourfold army; || 16 ||

Having been defeated by one superior to the supreme, and having reached the forest to practice austerities, he considers himself to have lived for an entire kalpa even for the duration of a mere moment. || 17 ||
In the same way, even during the waking state, he indulges in the kingdom of his desires;
due to the flow of the river of time, he does not perceive that his lifespan has been exhausted.
Like the sun covered by clouds, the Supreme Lord, greatly deluded by his own illusory power (māyā), appears to be a doer of little and a knower of little. (19)
Whatever one does or knows, in each of those acts, this Supreme Lord—the King, the Knower—is said to be the Sovereign by virtue of His own power. (20)
Since knowledge and action have been transferred through their identity with Śiva into all living beings,
the lordship of souls is established by virtue of that union with His power.
In various cognitions such as "this is a jar" and "this is a cloth," one's own cognition shines forth by itself, just like the light of the sun.
If knowledge were not self-established, the world would be blind darkness;
if it had no activity whatsoever, how could there be worldly transaction? (23)
Action, indeed, consists of the nature of vibration and transformation;
when external cognition vibrates, it arises like its sprout. (24)
Action depends upon that which is to be produced, that which is to be attained, that which is to be refined, and that which is to be transformed;
it is recognized [in such expressions] as "he makes," "he goes," "he wipes," and "he cuts. (25)

Śiva appears as omniscient within the bodies of Brahmā and others, while among gods, animals, and humans, he appears as possessing limited knowledge according to their respective degrees of gradation. (26)
The viviparous, the oviparous, the sweat-born, and the soil-born—these are the four kinds of bodies, each succeeding one being inferior in its functioning. || 27 ||
The conceptual construction extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is like a dream, once the unconditioned light of the Supreme Self has been directly realized. (28)
The Vedic statement, "Smaller than the small,
greater than the great," and the Rudra Upaniṣad as well, praise this Śiva, who is the self of all.
Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is the Lord, the Guru, and the Self, who is distinguished by various forms yet pervades the body like space.
Thus ends the summary of the first chapter in the *Mānasollāsa*, a treatise explaining the meaning of the *Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotra*. || 31 ||
The summary of the second chapter:

This world, which was previously free of conceptual construction like a sprout within a seed, is again rendered variegated by the diversity of the mental constructs of space and time fashioned by *māyā*.
Salutations to this Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who, like a master of illusion, expands himself at will, and who is like a great yogin; salutations to this embodiment of the venerable Guru. || 2 ||
The substrate of conceptual proliferation consists of atoms joined together;
therefore, a jar appears as being composed of clay, not as being composed of a Supreme Lord. || 1 ||
Qualities such as color, taste, and so forth, which reside in atoms themselves,
produce another quality of the same genus in the effect.

That in which the effect inheres is its inherent cause (samavāyi-kāraṇa); whereas that which is the instrument, such as the wheel and so forth, is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyi-kāraṇa) of the jar. (3)

That which resides in the inherent cause (samavāyin) and likewise resides in the substratum of the inherent cause, and whose capacity is ascertained with respect to the effect—that is postulated as the non-inherent cause (asamavāyin). (4)
The efficient cause (nimitta) and the material cause (kāraṇa) of these things is God, like a potter;
whatever effect arises from something, it remains established within that very thing. (5)
"A pot [arises] from clay, a cloth from thread, and a ring from gold"—thus say the Vaiśeṣikas, and likewise the Naiyāyikas as well. (6)
Rajas, sattva, and tamas—these are the three qualities (guṇas) of Pradhāna.
Among them, rajas is red and mobile; sattva is white and illuminating.
"Tamas is black and obscuring; [rajas and sattva] are the causes of creation, maintenance, and destruction"—thus the Sāṃkhyas declare, and their refutation is now stated.
The existence [of the effect] is admitted in all effects from the sprout up to the fruit;
from where have those particles come that are connected within the seeds of the banyan tree? (9)
It is agreed by all that the effect conforms to its cause;
therefore, existence and radiance follow along everywhere.
When a flower has turned into fruit, and when milk has reached the state of curd, qualities such as color, taste, and so forth, which belong to a different class, are perceived. (11)
Cause and effect, part and whole, genus and individual, quality and the possessor of quality, action and the agent—these and others are merely conceptual constructions of light itself. (12)
Consciousness is not admitted for atoms nor even for the Pradhāna;
for knowledge and action, which constitute the creation of the world, are seen to reside in a conscious substratum. (13)
Just as curd is produced from milk through the power of the action of time,
so the world arises in the form of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge through the power of consciousness.
Knowledge is twofold: non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka), which illuminates the mere object, and conceptual (savikalpaka), which is of many kinds because it illuminates names and so forth. (15)
Volition, doubt, error, memory, similarity, certainty, conjecture, indecision, and likewise other types of experience [are the objects of mental cognition]. (16)
The Cārvākas accept only perception; Kaṇāda and Sugata, moreover, accept inference as well; and the Sāṃkhyas accept those two as well as verbal testimony. (17)
Even those who perceive only the Nyāya system accept these [three], and some also include analogy;
Prabhākara, however, says that there are four, including presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). (18)

The followers of Bhaṭṭa and likewise the Vedāntins maintain that these [means of knowledge] have non-existence as the sixth; the Paurāṇikas, however, have declared them to include probability (sambhava) and tradition (aitihya). (19)
The followers of Kaṇāda declare that there are six categories: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence. (20)
The nine substances are the elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether—as well as space, time, the self, and the mind.

There are exactly twenty-four qualities: the five beginning with sound, [color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, weight, fluidity, viscidity, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort]. (21)
Dimension, number, the two—conjunction and disjunction—separateness by its own nature, gravity, and furthermore, fluidity. (22)
Remoteness, proximity, viscidity, momentum, as well as cognition, aversion, pleasure, pain, desire, merit, demerit, and effort. (23)
Formative force (saṃskāra) is threefold: velocity (vega), which is the cause of motion in things such as arrows;
and mental impression (bhāvanā), which is the cause of recollection of objects seen, heard, or experienced. (24)
That which is called *sthitasthāpakatā* (elasticity) is the cause of restoring a thing to its previous state;
it is clearly perceived in cases such as birch bark or tree branches that have been pulled [and released]. (25)
The wise declare that action is fivefold: throwing upward, throwing downward, going, stretching out, and contracting. (26)
Generality is said to be of two kinds: the higher and the lower.
The higher is existence itself (sattā) alone, which persists as the underlying thread throughout everything.
Substantiality, as well as quality-ness and so forth, are likewise lower universals;
the particulars are infinite, and they are the causes of the cognition of exclusion.
Just as the relation of color to a pot is eternal and inherent (samavāya), so too are time, space, direction, and the self eternal and all-pervading. (29)
The atoms are of four kinds, limited, and eternal;
thus, in the Vaiśeṣika system, six categories of existence are proclaimed. (30)

Māyā, Pradhāna, the Unmanifest (avyakta), ignorance (avidyā), non-knowledge (ajñāna), the Imperishable (akṣara), the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta), Primordial Matter (prakṛti), and Darkness (tamas)—these are its designations. || 31 ||
Due to the attachment of the reflection of Brahman-consciousness within Māyā, there arise Mahat, Kāla, and Puruṣa; from the principle of Mahat, Ahaṃkāra arises. || 32 ||
From the *ahaṅkāra* characterized by *tamas*, ether, air, fire, water, and earth arise;
and from them, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell follow in sequence. (33)
The objects of the senses and the qualities of the elements are yours;
likewise are the gods—Sadāśiva, Īśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and the Four-faced One.
From the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the internal organs and the sense organs arise;
the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*) constitute the internal instruments (*karaṇa*).
Doubt, certainty, pride, and recollection—these are the objects;
the Moon, Prajāpati, Rudra, and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) are the presiding deities. || 36 ||
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are known as the organs of cognition;
the deities traditionally assigned to them are said to be the quarters, wind, the sun, Varuṇa, and the two Aśvins.
From the *ahaṃkāra* characterized by *rajas*, the vital breaths that impel the organs of action arise;
these organs of action are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ. (38)
Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure are known as the objects;
their presiding deities are Agni, Indra, Upendra, Yama, and Kāma. (39)
The vital breaths are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna; together with the five elements and the fourteen sense organs. || 40 ||
Those who know the Sāṅkhya scriptures recognize twenty-four principles:
Mahat, Kāla, Pradhāna, Māyā, Vidya, and Puruṣa; || 41 ||
Thus the experts in the Purāṇas have declared that there are thirty principles (tattvas);
along with these are Bindu and Nāda, Śakti and Śiva, and beyond that, Śānta and Atīta.
The experts in the Śaiva Āgamas have declared that there are thirty-six principles (tattvas).
All conceptual constructions (vikalpas) previously existed within the Self, like a sprout within a seed. (43)
These have been manifested by Māyā in the form of will, knowledge, and action, because all activities are preceded by will, knowledge, and action. || 44 ||
Therefore, it is certain that all living beings are from the Lord;
from a seed comes a tree, and from the tree a seed is produced through a continuous succession. (45)
To dispel such doubt, the example of the yogis is cited:
"Viśvāmitra and others of old had their meditative absorption fully ripened. (46)
Free from the need for material causes, instruments, or purposes,
they created by their own will a creation enriched with all enjoyments.
The Lord, possessing infinite power, is independent and requires nothing else;
by his mere will, he creates, sustains, and destroys the entire universe.
The Lord would not be an eternal agent by virtue of the activity of causal factors,
nor would He be a knower by virtue of the activity of means of valid cognition, for He is self-luminous.
Even his state of being a knower is merely his agency due to his absolute sovereignty;
and whatever variety of power of will he possesses is his capacity for acting according to his own free will.
Who here is able to limit the independent will of the Lord, which He may choose to actuate, not to actuate, or to actuate otherwise? (51)
And scripture, through the passage "He desired," declares that the creation of the Lord proceeds from desire;
and it further states, "From that Self, space was produced. (52)
If the Supreme Lord were merely the instrumental cause of this world, then it would possess the qualities of being subject to modification and destruction, just like a potter’s [clay]. (53)
If the nine qualities, beginning with intellect (buddhi), are indeed eternal for the Lord, then He, possessing eternal will, would surely engage in the creation of the world at all times. (54)
Because there would be no cessation of activity, saṃsāra would never perish;
the instruction on liberation would be in vain, and even the sacred scripture (āgama) would be meaningless. || 55 ||
Therefore, this agency of the Lord over the world is a play of māyā;
even the conventional practice of teaching bondage and liberation proceeds through māyā.
Thus ends the summary of the second chapter in the *Mānasollāsa*, a treatise explaining the meaning of the *Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotra*.
The summary of the third chapter:
He whose manifestation, being of the nature of existence, appears as the object of that which is like the unreal;
and who, by means of the Vedic word "That thou art," directly awakens those who have taken refuge in him.
Salutations to that venerable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the embodiment of the Guru, through the direct realization of whom there shall be no more returning to the ocean of worldly existence. || 3 ||
When entities have come together through the radiance of existence, from where have they come?
Thus questioned, according to the analogy of a reflection in a mirror and so forth, one is awakened. (1)
In entities that are unreal fictions, insentient, and momentary in their destruction,
existence and luminosity are transmitted from the eternal Lord.
The very existence of these entities is their own existence, and there is nothing beyond that;
likewise, their manifestation is nothing more than the manifestation of the Self. (3)
The various forms of cognitions and their objects as well are attached to the ego-sense, like clusters of gems upon a string. (4)
This entire universe appears as non-different from the Light; it has no existence separate from it, just as waves, bubbles, and the like have no existence apart from water. || 5 ||
That knowledge which exists by entering into objects as "I know," subsequently comes to rest within the inner self as "it has been known by me."
Just as effects such as jars find their rest in clay and other materials,
so too the universe, being non-different from Light, finds its rest in the Supreme Lord.
Just as a mirror is soiled by its own inherent blackness.
Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded.

Just as the space within a jar and the great space [of the universe] are distinguished by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the jar, so too is the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) produced by the limiting adjunct of the body. 9.
By such statements as "That thou art," the identity of those two is demonstrated;
for when it is said, "This is that man," a single person is indeed perceived. (10)
That reality which is the cause of the world is called the meaning of the word *tat*;
whereas the individual soul (*jīva*), delimited by the body and so forth, is designated by the word *tvam*. (11)
That which was perceived at a particular place, time, state, and so forth, is called "that";
likewise, that which is perceived at this place, time, and so forth, is designated as "this. (12)
Setting aside this primary distinction between the two words, [the compound] indicates a single human being, just as the expression "this man" (so 'yaṃ pumān) does. (13)
Having abandoned both inwardness and outwardness, the statement "That thou art" likewise indicates the oneness of the individual self and the supreme self.
In this context, the relationship between two words is called grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya);
the relationship between the word-meanings would be that of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatva). || 15 ||
Through the conjunction of the indicated object (lakṣya) and the indicator (lakṣaṇa), the sentence conveys both [the literal meaning] and oneness;
like the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges," there is no *jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication). || 16 ||
Nor can there be a non-abandoning secondary sense (ajahallakṣaṇā) in the case of sentences such as "The white one runs";
rather, the secondary sense of sentences like "That thou art" is one of partial indication (bhāgalakṣaṇā). || 17 ||
Thus, as in the case of sentences such as "This is that person," the application of words with distinct grounds for their usage to a single entity has been described. (18)
In this context, "functioning" (pravṛtti) is said to mean having a common substratum;
the individual soul (jīva) is not described by the statement as being either a part or a modification of the Supreme. (19)
Because He has entered into the forms created by His own *māyā* as the individual soul (*jīvātman*), He is understood through both scripture and reasoning to be partless and changeless. (20)
Just as the space within a jar is neither a modification nor a part of the infinite sky, the statement "You are Indra" is certainly not intended as mere praise. (21)
This statement is not intended to express similarity, as in the case of "the boy is fire," nor is it a proof of the relation of cause and effect, as in the case of "the clay and the jar. || 22 ||

The genus is not the indicator of the individual; the statement is not like "the cow Khaṇḍa," nor is this sentence composed of quality and qualified substance, as in the case of "blue lotus" and the like. (23)
A statement [identifying Brahman] with respect to [the body] is not intended for worship, as in the case of the cognition of the Lord in an image;
nor is it figurative, as in the case of "the king's man" [being called the king]. // 24 //
For it is heard that this Lord has entered [the world] as the individual soul (jīvātman) within the aggregate of the body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego. (25)
The ignorant establish the existence of a self through the synthesis of [the aggregates], just as the cognition of fire arises from the synthesis of wood, iron, and so forth. (26)
Having entered the sheath consisting of food, the Self manifests as the body—stout, young, emaciated, dark-complexioned, and characterized by the distinctions of caste and stage of life. (27)
"I live even within the sheath of the vital breaths; I am hungry and thirsty.
Thus, one thinks with certainty and conviction within the mental sheath (manomaya-kośa). 28.
Abiding in the sheath consisting of consciousness, it remains with the thought "I cognize";
yet, within the ego-sense known as the sheath consisting of bliss, it exists due to past actions.
He rejoices, thinking, "I am made happy by merits and acts of worship," thus enveloped by these sheaths as if by five coverings.
Although the Supreme Lord is all-pervading, he appears as if limited,
just as the sun, having entered the water, appears manifold.
Likewise, having entered bodies, the Lord manifests in many ways;
being the cause and being the effect are the incidental characteristics of those two.
This view is not at all primary, like the notion that "the moon is on the branch";
rather, what is called "Great Light" is the very nature characterized as the moon. (33)
The nature of those two is their essential character, which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
the identity of these two, which share this single characteristic, is established by the Great Sentence.
Therefore, it is established that being the self of all consists in being a single light;
for gods, animals, and humans, there is no existence separate from that light. || 35 ||
Because the individual soul (jīva) is non-different from light, it is designated as the "Self of all.
Thus, when the realization of its nature as light is firmly established, [it becomes the Self of all]. (36)
One attains the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya) from which there is no return,
even if one has encountered it but once by chance, through the realization of the self-nature of all things.
Freed from all evil, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
That great-souled one whose contemplation of the universal self (sarvātmabhāvanā) has reached full maturity is himself the Supreme Lord, the manifest deliverer from saṃsāra. || 38 ||
Thus ends the summary of the third chapter in the *Mānasollāsa*, a treatise explaining the meaning of the *Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotra*. 39.
The Summary of the Fourth Chapter:
His knowledge, radiant with the light of a great lamp situated within the interior of a jar containing various apertures, vibrates outwardly through the doors of the instruments such as the eyes.
"I know"—it is to Him alone, shining thus, that this entire world reflects its light; salutations to that Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the form of the venerable Guru. || 4 ||
"Entities such as jars and cloths manifest because they are inherently existent, not due to the penetration of God (īśvara); to this, the following reply is given. (1)
If the synthesizer of the thought "I" did not flash forth as "I know," then what would manifest for whom? The world would be like deep sleep. || 2 ||

The existence of non-existent things does not occur by themselves either before or after; nor does it exist in the present by its own nature. Therefore, existence resides in the Lord, who is devoid of prior and posterior states.
If insentient things were to manifest by themselves without a Lord,
then everything would appear to everyone, or else nothing at all would appear.
Therefore, the world would be either entirely omniscient or entirely ignorant, for there would be no distinction between the insentient and the sentient if both were equally self-luminous. (5)
It would follow that the states of being the grasped and the grasper, and so forth, would be identical;
furthermore, because there would be no restriction of the sense organs, tastes and other objects would become visible to the eye.

The two portions of the internal organ, consisting of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), are like the rear and front parts of a mirror that is both stained and unstained. || 7 ||
The Lord, manifesting within the reflection, is called the agent and the knower;
the intellect, due to the predominance of the quality of *sattva*, is like a stainless mirror. (8)
Through the power of its own reflection, it assumes the shadow of the objects;
likewise, through its connection with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), all the sense organs [assume their respective shadows]. || 9 ||
The channels are fixed within the internal organ like pegs driven into the rim of a chariot wheel,
or like threads woven together with water.
By means of those beautiful orbs, all the organs proceed toward their respective objects like sparks of fire.
The central location of the body is called the *mūlādhāra*;
it is situated two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis.
It is triangular, with its apex pointing downward, resembling the womb of a maiden;
therein is established the supreme power named Kuṇḍalinī. || 13 ||
That Sarasvatī is the progenitor of the vital breath (prāṇa), the fire (agni), the point (bindu), and the sound (nāda);
she resides at the tip of the corner of the Mūlādhāra and goes to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) via the Suṣumnā.
At its base, it resembles a bamboo stalk cut in half, endowed with six supports;
on its two side corners, the two channels Iḍā and Piṅgalā are situated.
They call it the "wheel of channels" (nāḍīcakra), from which the channels have emerged;
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā run toward the ends of the eyes.
Woven together by the network of channels (nāḍīcakra), both [channels] extend as far as the tip of the nose;
resting upon the navel-center, they are situated like a hen’s egg.
They call it the "wheel of channels" (*nāḍīcakra*); from it, the channels have emerged.
The channel named Pūṣā and the channel Alambuṣā resort to both ears;
from there, the channel called Śuklā extends to the middle of the eyebrows.
The channel named Sarasvatī extends to the tip of the tongue and spreads speech;
the channel named Viśvodarī consumes the fourfold food.
Having drunk the water from the milk-yielding [cow], she causes a sneeze when it reaches the throat;
three channels have arisen from the wheel of channels and are directed downwards.
Rākā emits semen, Sinīvālī urine, and Kuhū excretes feces;
furthermore, the Śaṅkhinī vessel takes up the essence of the food consumed.
Having entered the hollow of the skull, it collects the nectar at the crown of the head.
There are one hundred and one channels, and among them, one extends to the head.
"Ascending from those two, one becomes liberated"—such is the teaching of the Vedānta.
When, impelled by merits residing in the intellect, [the soul] proceeds through the path of the senses... (23)
When one experiences objects such as sound and the rest, then that is the waking state.
When these senses have been withdrawn, the person [experiences] those born from the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the waking state.
When one experiences mental objects, that is the state of dreaming;
the withdrawal of even the mind is called deep sleep (suṣupti). || 25 ||
Therein, the person exists as pure being, yet concealed by māyā;
through the influence of māyā, he appears as "deluded," "insentient," and "ignorant. (26)
At the time of awakening, the person, being of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, shines forth perfectly, thinking, "I slept happily. (27)
When the Great Lord thus enters and manifests the world, even the sun and other luminaries shine; how much more so, then, other things such as jars? (28)
Therefore, existence and manifestation belong to entities because they have the Lord as their support;
thus, Brahman is taught by the Śruti as "Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. (29)
Everything arising from the waking and dreaming states is unreal and insentient, like a blind man;
yet the thought "I am the Lord" shines forth in all living beings. (30)
I am threefold: non-conceptual, pure, and impure.
The non-conceptual is the supreme Brahman, from which all mental constructions have been shaken off. (31)
At the time of discernment, it is pure through the removal of the body and other such factors, resembling the sky when it is freed from dust, darkness, smoke, and clouds. (32)
Just as the atmosphere, when contracted by the stars, is seen only slightly, so too [the Self] is made impure and turbid through association with the body, senses, and other such factors. (33)
Just as space, when enveloped by darkness, appears to vibrate as if devoid of room, so too when the individual soul awakens to its divine nature as "I," [it perceives itself thus]. 34.
Then the individual soul (jīva) will become omniscient and the creator of all;
deluded by Māyā, it is through Vidyā that the Lord (Īśa) shines forth.
When there is a continuous flow of non-conceptualization, the true Self shines forth;
upon the removal of the obscuration known as ignorance, this Supreme Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti manifests by Himself. (36)
Thus ends the summary of the fourth chapter in the *Mānasollāsa*, a treatise explaining the meaning of the *Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotra*. || 37 ||
The Summary of the Fifth Chapter:

Those who argue with great delusion, like women, children, the blind, and the dull-witted, know the body, the vital breath, the senses, and even the flickering intellect as the void, while thinking "I am."
Salutation to that Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is the embodiment of the venerable Guru, the destroyer of the great delusion fashioned by the playful manifestation of the power of Māyā. || 5 ||
Perception is the sole means of valid cognition; reality consists of the four elements;
liberation is nothing other than death; and sensual pleasure and wealth are the two goals of human life. (1)
Indeed, God is not the creator, and talk of the next world is in vain;
if the self exists apart from the body, let it be seen here before us like a jar.
For the body is seen as short, tall, young, or a child; it exists, is born, transforms, grows old, declines, decays, and dies. (3)
Thus have been described the six modifications of being which reside in the body;
and the division of castes and stages of life is likewise established solely within bodies. (4)
The sacraments, such as the birth-rite and others, are prescribed for the body alone;
they offer the auspicious blessing, "May he live for a hundred years," for the sake of the body. (5)
Thus the dull-witted Cārvāka deceives himself with such proliferation:
"I breathe, I live, I am hungry, I am thirsty. (6)
By the force of such cognitions as these, some consider the soul to be the agent of perception, thinking:
"I hear, I see, I smell, and I taste. (7)
Others have declared that the self is the intellect (buddhi), which they recognize as being superior to the sense-faculties on the strength of the cognition "I know. (8)
The refutation of those whose minds are deluded by illusion is now stated:
[the refutation] of the body and other insentient objects, which are non-self like stones. (9)
How could the sense of "I-ness" exist without immersion into the Lord?
This body, for its part, is not the Self, because it is an object of perception and because it is insentient. (10)
Because it possesses form and so forth, because it has parts, and because it is composed of the elements, it is like a jar.
Even in fainting, deep sleep, and death, the body is still perceived. || 11 ||

Because it is distinct from the body and other such things, the Self does not manifest at that time, just as the sun, though the primordial cause of the activities of the world, [is not perceived]. || 12 ||
In the same way, the person (puruṣa) is the supreme cause for the activity of the body and so forth;
even women, children, and the blind think, "This is my body. (13)
No one ever perceives "I am the body";
nor are the sense organs the Self, because they are instruments, like a lamp. (14)
The ear is the instrument for perceiving sound, like the sound of a lute or other musical instruments;
the eye is the instrument for perceiving form, like the triad of light. || 15 ||
The nose is the perceiver of odor, like a flower-casket and the like;
the tongue is the perceiver of taste, like curd, honey, clarified butter, and so forth. || 16 ||
"I have no sense organs; I am mute, blind, and deaf"—do people who speak thus, being devoid of sense organs, lack a self? (17)
The vital breath (prāṇa) also is not the Self, because of the absence of knowledge during deep sleep;
[the Self exists] for the purpose of bringing about the cessation of the fatigue arising from the enjoyment of the waking and dreaming states.
When deep sleep has come upon the person, the vital breath (prāṇa) alone moves in order to protect the body and for the sake of experiencing the remaining karma.

If it is argued that the insentience of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs there because the instruments have ceased [to function], then how can there be a cessation of the instruments while the vital breath is still active? (20)
For when the sovereign is intent on battle, the soldiers do not cease;
therefore, the vital breath cannot be the master of the instruments [of action]. (21)
When the Person who impels the mind ceases [its activity], all the instruments (karaṇa) cease from that point; therefore, the Person is their master.
But for the Buddhist, [consciousness] is momentary, perceivable, and endowed with coming and going;
illuminated by the reflection of the self, it illuminates the world. (23)
Cognition arises in the self and dissolves in the self alone;
being non-existent before and after, cognition does not establish itself by its own power.
If the successive arising [of cognitions] occurs from each preceding cognition, then it would follow that there is the simultaneous occurrence of many cognitions in every moment. (25)
Another cognition would not arise, because destruction is non-existent;
if the self were the aggregate of these [elements], then when one part is separated, [the self would cease to exist]. (26)
In that case, consciousness would not follow as a consequence, because there is no composite whole;
for [a collection] consisting of a multitude of distinct conscious beings would possess different perceptions, movements, and intentions. (27)
This [body] would either break apart immediately or become inactive;
for it is understood that the Self, even though situated within the body, is all-pervading. (28)
If this [self] were of atomic dimension, it could not pervade the entire body;
if it were of the dimension of the body, there would be no state of childhood, old age, and so forth.
If [the self] were subject to transformation like the body, it would perish just like it, through the transformation of karmas into the forms of worms, elephants, and so forth. (30)
Because it is all-pervasive, the Self enters into jars and other objects like space;
it is manifested even in the mind, though that mind is the size of an atom.
In a dream, the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings is established within the Self alone;
the delusion that "I" am the body and so forth is the cause of saṃsāra.
"The Teacher has entered within," thus the Śruti teaches for the sake of liberation;
in this way, this Great Māyā deludes even the disputants.

Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is of the nature of knowledge and bliss, whose true form is far removed from the ego, and who, upon being directly realized, immediately dissolves into Sadāśiva, transcending body, senses, and vital breath. || 34 ||
Thus ends the summary of the fifth chapter in the *Mānasollāsa*, a treatise explaining the meaning of the *Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotra*. || 35 ||
The summary of the sixth chapter:
That person who, due to the concealment by *māyā*, resembles the sun or moon eclipsed by Rāhu,
becomes one consisting of pure existence (*sanmātra*) during deep sleep through the withdrawal of the instruments of perception.
Salutations to this Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the embodiment of the venerable Guru, who is recognized at the time of awakening by the thought, "I slept previously. 6.

If it is argued that just as the universe is contained within [the self] in a dream, so it is also in the waking state, then in deep sleep what appears to whom, and who is the enduring conscious being there? (1)
Everything is momentary and empty; everything indeed consists of its own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa). The aggregates of atoms—earth, water, fire, and air—[are likewise such].
The bodies of humans and others are an aggregation of the five aggregates (skandhas);
and the aggregates are form, consciousness, perception, mental formations, and feeling. (3)
They are called "forms" (rūpa) because they are manifested; this includes both objects and the sense faculties.
The cognition of these objects and faculties is termed the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha). || 4 ||
The Sugatas have declared that the conceptualization of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is fivefold, consisting of perceptions distinguished by name, quality, action, and genus. (5)
The term "cow" (gauḥ) is said to be the designation for cows; however, the universal "cowness" (gotva) resides within the cow.
Its qualities, such as whiteness and so forth, as well as its actions, such as going and so forth, likewise [reside there].
Having horns, four feet, and a tail—this is indeed a specific cognition.
Thus, that which is established as fivefold is called the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha). //7//
Attachment and the like, as well as merit and demerit, are called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
Pleasure, pain, and liberation constitute the aggregate known as feeling (vedanāskandha). || 8 ||
There is no self whatsoever other than the five aggregates;
there is no Lord who is the creator, for the world possesses its own inherent excellence.
From the aggregates and from momentary atoms, [the subsequent] moment arises;
indeed, each succeeding moment would arise from each preceding moment alone. (10)

For indeed, from that very same prior cognition, a subsequent cognition arises; the notion that "this is that very same thing" is an error, just like [the illusion that] "this is that same flame. (11)
The Self is conceptualized as both self and non-self by those deluded by the notions "it exists" and "it shines";
for, being devoid of rejection or acquisition, does space ever manifest? 12.
Thus, the Buddhist proponent is refuted as he speaks:
"If emptiness is the cause of the world, the world itself cannot be established. (13)
By whom is it established that "the pot is empty" and "the cloth is empty"?
If emptiness did not manifest at all, the world would not appear, just like a rabbit's horn. (14)
Seeking wealth, what would one take up? Seeking a burden, what would one discard?
Who could perform an action or prohibit one, given the emptiness of both the object and the self? (15)
If there were no one to assemble the aggregates and atoms, this entire world would sink into nothingness; therefore, such a person must exist. (16)
Inert objects such as jars and cloths do not arise without a cause;
yet the deluded person thinks, "May I become one of great power. (17)
Why does the Buddhist who denies the self practice religious vows?
If recognition were an illusion, how could there be eating and so forth? (18)
"Even a child, having determined that 'this food is indeed the means to achieve what is desired, just like the food of previous days,' proceeds to eat and so forth. (19)
Just as providing space is the purposeful activity (arthakriyā) of space, so too are agency, cognition, and so forth the purposeful activities of the person (puruṣa). 20.
Even at the time of deep sleep, the Self consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss, because it is recognized [upon waking] by the thought, "I slept happily. (21)
The formulation "it is recognized" (pratyabhijñāyate) is used in the sense of the reflexive object-agent (karmakartṛ).
Because it is self-luminous, the Self knows itself by itself. (22)
In deep sleep, being deluded by Māyā, he appears as if dull and blind;
yet he shines both through his lack of luminosity and through his own self-luminosity.
And the Lord is directly distinguished within the insentient body and so forth;
this very power of the Great Lord is called the delusive *māyā*. (24)
The removal of delusion for the cognizers is designated as liberation;
it is free from the three states and undisturbed by defects and the like. (25)

Like a blade of grass, he consists of pure existence; like the seed-pod of a banyan tree, he is free from external and internal petals; and like the core of a plantain trunk, he is devoid of outer and inner layers. (26)
Partless, changeless, without appearance, and stainless—
the Puruṣa, solitary and complete, is called the Supreme Lord.
Where speech turns back and where the mind dissolves,
there indeed all beings and worlds become one.
And all the principles are like rivers in the ocean;
what grief, what delusion can there be for one who perceives that oneness? (29)
Although this [consciousness] exists as conceptual due to its nature as the signified and the signifier, it can become non-conceptual through the exclusion of the body and so forth. (30)
If a wise person knows that Brahman is non-existent, he becomes non-existent himself;
but if he knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing. 31.
Thus ends the summary of the sixth chapter in the *Mānasollāsa*, a treatise that elucidates the meaning of the *Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotra*.
The Summary of the Seventh Chapter:
That which persists even through childhood and other stages, as well as through the states of waking and so forth— even amidst all changing conditions— is the "I," which always flashes forth within.
Salutation to this Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the embodiment of the venerable Guru, who reveals his own self to those who worship him by means of the auspicious mudrā. || 7 ||
If the self is determined to be permanent on the strength of recognition, what indeed is this recognition, or what is its purpose? (1)
Recognition is not enumerated among the means of valid cognition, such as perception;
one who asks how it can possess the status of a valid means of knowledge is thus instructed. (2)
The synthesis of "this is that very same [object]" regarding some previously perceived entity that is now appearing is called recognition (pratyabhijñāna). (3)
Having set aside the incidental differences of place, time, form, and so forth, that which is perceived as a single, continuous entity is designated by the expression "this is that. (4)

By the removal of such qualities as "limited knowledge" (kiñcijjñatva) that arise from association with illusion (māyā), the cognition of omniscience and other attributes constitutes the self-recognition (pratyabhijñāna) of the Self. || 5 ||
Due to the recollection of objects experienced in a previous birth, the young fawn proceeds of its own accord to drink its mother’s milk.
Therefore, it is certain that the self is permanent even across different bodies,
because an infant’s drinking of breast milk would not be possible without memory.
Existing previously at the time of experience and later at the time of recollection,
the self, in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), remembers the object established within itself.
If it is asserted that recognition is simply the memory of entities, then how could memory serve as a means of valid cognition for the stability of the self? (9)
In memory, there is no manifestation of the object, nor is there any ascertainment of the object;
furthermore, it cannot occur between the experience of the object and [the memory] themselves, just as it cannot occur between two fingers. (10)

If it is argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that, like a staff, an object qualified by its experience [would be perceived] everywhere in the same way, then listen.

When the previous experience has perished, memory arises from the causal complex known as the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), which is supported by that [experience] and produced by human effort. || 12 ||
When the experience that was to be made known has perished, it causes the self—the cognizer of that [experience]—to be aware of its object as something imperishable. (13)
When the object has been forgotten or when the experience has perished,
the Lord, who is never himself subject to forgetfulness, remembers the object as resting within Himself.
The delusion of the perceivers is produced by Māyā through darkness;
Māyā and Vidya are the powers of the Lord, comparable to the shadow and the light of the sun. (15)
One should not conceal objects with illusion; rather, having distracted them, one should reveal them through knowledge.
Indeed, recognition alone is the means of proof for all instruments of valid cognition.
Having dispelled through knowledge the illusion (māyā) that creates the sense of separation—namely, "The Lord is one and I am another"—there arises the recollection: "I am the Lord. (17)
The Lord, veiled by the curtain of Māyā, was only slightly manifest;
when the covering was completely removed, He shone forth like the thousand-rayed sun.
There is no operation of causes, nor indeed of the means of valid cognition; what is called "recognition" is nothing other than the removal of delusion. (19)
Whatever measures exist for the sake of worldly transaction, no other function is found for them than the removal of delusion. (20)

The attributes of the body—insentience, unreality, and limitation—are superimposed through delusion upon the conscious Self, which is in truth the nature of existence, knowledge, and bliss; yet this same nature of existence, knowledge, and bliss is likewise falsely attributed to the body.
Just as one is deluded by the thought "this is silver" regarding a mother-of-pearl shell,
if that very [silver] were to appear [as real], your theory of dissolution would not be established.
An absolutely non-existent thing, such as a man’s horn, could never manifest anywhere.
In the case of an error, there may be a recollection such as "this is silver" regarding a beloved's hand and so forth.
If this error were due to similarity, such that one would think "this is equal to that," then there would be no equality in cases such as "the conch is yellow" or "sugar is bitter. (24)
If the mother-of-pearl were to manifest as silver through identity (tādātmya), then there would be an error without a substratum and a sublation that is without limit. || 25 ||
If silver established in consciousness were perceived as being external, then it would follow that the body would be burned when fire is superimposed upon a guñjā berry and the like. (26)
Because it is a manifestation devoid of logical justification, error has no defining characteristic;
for if it were to possess some defining characteristic, error itself could not be established. (27)
Just as the moon in water, as the snake in a rope in a place free from fear, and as bracelets and the like in their cause, gold; so [is it perceived]. (28)
Like silver in what is grasped as such, like a city of yakṣas pervading the empty sky, like water in a ray of light, or like a thief in an inactive post that merely appears to be moving. (29)
This entire universe, which is a false construction, is superimposed upon the Self through delusion;
yet the Self is self-luminous, of the nature of existence, and free from both error and sublation.
When delusion has been dispelled, the reality is recognized as it was before;
once the limiting adjuncts such as the body have been shaken off, the Self alone remains as the Great Lord. || 31 ||
Memory, perception, tradition, and other such means of valid cognition as well, [the author] declares to be the word of a reliable authority for the sake of establishing recognition. (32)
Thus ends the summary of the seventh chapter in the *Mānasollāsa*, a treatise explaining the meaning of the *Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotra*. 33.
The summary of the eighth chapter:

One perceives the universe through the distinction of cause and effect, through the relationship of master and servant, likewise through that of disciple and teacher, and in the form of father and son, and so forth.
Whether in dream or in waking, this person is deluded by māyā; to him, the embodiment of the venerable Guru, to this Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, be this salutation. || 8 ||
If there is no object whatsoever apart from manifestation, how can worldly convention exist, which culminates in the instruction of ultimate reality? (1)
For one who asks thus: "Whose are bondage and liberation? By what cause is one bound? And what would be the characteristic of illusion (māyā)? (2)
One should be capable of answering and easily comprehending the reply.
The meaning already stated in seven verses is now recounted again in brief. (3)
In this case, tautology—whether by way of word or meaning—is not a fault;
rather, through repetition, the greater importance of the matter is conveyed. (4)
Even though the Supreme Lord is one, self-luminous, and of the nature of pure existence,
there are manifold conceptual constructions such as the relationship between cause and effect.
"The head of Rāhu is a cavity; my own self is the body of the ether"—such conceptualizations are similar in that they do not have distinct, external objects as their domain. (6)
Through the relationship of the worshipped and the worshipper, through the succession of teacher and disciple,
and in the form of master and servant and so forth, the Lord sports according to His own will.
He who is a son with respect to his father is indeed the father himself with respect to his son;
for that which is one alone is conceived as if manifold merely through words.
Therefore, in the investigation of ultimate reality, there exists only luminosity;
the perception of difference is merely false, imagined within the self through illusion.
Falsehood (mithyātva) means being sublated when right knowledge arises;
then the teacher, the disciple, the instruction, and so forth, appear like a dream. (10)
Even though the Vedānta is itself illusory, it can awaken one to the Truth, just as an image of a deity, a painting, or a reflection [conveys the reality of what they represent]. (11)
This entire worldly transaction is the manifestation of Māyā;
Māyā, which resembles deep sleep, is sublated by one's own awakening.
The designation for that which manifests devoid of logical justification is called "māyā.
It is not non-existent, since it is perceived; nor is it existent, since it is sublated. (13)
This [ignorance] is not distinct from light and so forth, like the dark shadow of the sun;
nor is it non-distinct, because of its insentience; and due to contradiction, it cannot be of the nature of both. (14)
Because it lacks its own causes and constituent parts, this [nature] is not said to be composed of parts; yet, though devoid of parts itself, it is endowed with parts within its effects. (15)
This illusory courtesan, established only when left unexamined, deceives man indeed with her own false delusions. (16)
No one desires the severance of its root; for those who hold such a view, how could liberation of the mind ever be possible? (17)
The three states of the mind—waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—revolve like a wheel, serving as the sole cause for the delusion of duality. (18)
Through those [faculties] it performs actions, and by them again the mind is bound;
the Supreme Person, like the sun, is the solitary witness of the mind.
Just as the sun is not bound by the actions performed by living beings, so too the Self is not bound by the actions of the mind, because it is the witness. || 20 ||
"The self performs actions and is bound or liberated by them"—this conventional designation is merely a product of delusion alone. (21)
Just as the sun, though untouched by smoke, clouds, dust, or mist,
appears as if it were obscured, so too does the Self appear through māyā.
Just as some young boy, being made to spin by the force of play, perceives the world spinning and the expanse of the sky filled with a hundred moons; || 23 ||
In the very same way, the individual soul (jīva), deluded by illusion through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), perceives this manifold universe as it revolves in error. || 24 ||
Having united with the mind, the Lord appears as if moving along,
just as the sun, through contact with water, appears as if moving when it is not.
That person by whom the mind has been rendered objectless through the power of the practice of yoga becomes liberated while living, having ceased from worldly activity. || 26 ||
"Two birds, inseparable companions, exist; by means of Māyā, Śiva, delighting in the one unborn [Prakṛti], appears as manyfold—thus says the Śruti. (27)
Thus ends the summary of the eighth chapter in the *Mānasollāsa*, a treatise explaining the meaning of the *Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotra*. || 28 ||
The Summary of the Ninth Chapter: Earth, water,
fire, air, ether, the sun, the moon, and the individual soul— this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, appears as the eightfold form of Him alone.
For those who investigate, nothing else whatsoever exists apart from that all-pervading Supreme Lord;
to Him, the venerable Guru-form, the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti, be this salutation. || 9 ||
For one who asks how such an illusion might be brought to an end, the means for that is proclaimed as the practice of worshiping the Lord. (1)
Within the forms of the Supreme Lord, which consist of the thirty-six principles,
the eightfold forms are perceived directly by everyone.
Therefore, because the mind is not able to ascend quickly to the immeasurables,
the Guru teaches the contemplation of the Universal Self as consisting of the eight forms.
Within the body of Virāṭ, within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and even within the physical forms of living beings,
the aggregate of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) persists everywhere.
The pervasion of the mind, which is of an individualized form, occurs within this individual body;
therefore, one should contemplate this own body as being the self of all.
"Through the individual meditation (vyaṣṭy-upāsanā), a person shall attain pervasion of the collective (samaṣṭi).
Thus he taught ten times, saying, "He approaches [it]. (6)
Within the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr are traditionally taught;
they reside within the foundational centers (ādhāras) from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
The neck of the lute is Mount Meru, and the bones are the principal mountain ranges;
the Gaṅgā is the piṅgalā channel, while the Yamunā is proclaimed to be the iḍā.

Sarasvatī is said to be the Suṣumṇā; the other meritorious rivers are the [other] channels (nāḍīs). The seven elements (dhātus) are the islands (dvīpas), and sweat, tears, and so forth are the oceans. || 9 ||
The fire of time (kālāgni) resides in the root; the submarine fire (bāḍaba) is in the midst of the bones;
the lightning-fire (vaidyutāgni) is in the suṣumnā; and the earthly fire (pārthivāgni) is in the circle of the navel.
The fire of the sun resides in the heart, and the lunar orb in the skull;
they say that the other stars are the sense organs, such as the eyes and so forth.
Just as the worlds are supported by the winds such as the Pravahaṇa,
so too is the body sustained by the ten kinds of vital breaths, beginning with Prāṇa.
Having reached the iḍā and piṅgalā, the prāṇa, from the root in the form of the sun,
goes out through the two nostrils and dissolves at a distance of twelve finger-breadths.
The essence of the moon, measuring eight finger-breadths, enters within through the two channels; the apāna wind then expels the impurities, urine, flatus, and semen to the outside.

Having become composed of fire and moon and having resorted to the aperture of the *suṣumnā*, the *udāna* breath increases of its own accord as it ascends toward the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). || 15 ||
Vyāna pervades the body day after day with the essence of the food consumed;
Samāna, for its part, constantly provides fuel for the bodily fire.
Nāga causes hiccuping; Kūrma causes the opening and closing of the eyes; Kṛkara produces sneezing; and Devadatta causes yawning.
Fire produces grossness and does not abandon even that which is dead;
space provides room both outside and within. || 18 ||
The moon and sun are the leaders of time; for embodied beings, they are the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
The Puruṣa is the witness—thus is this body composed of eight forms.
The yogi who practices this worship with the mind, being disciplined in the eightfold yoga, attains the state beyond the mind. 20.
Clarity of mind, contentment, silence, restraint of the senses, compassion, courtesy, faith, straightforwardness, gentleness, and forgiveness. || 21 ||
Purity of being, non-violence, celibacy, mindfulness, and fortitude—these and other such qualities are known as the restraints (yamās) to be accomplished by the mind. || 22 ||
Bathing, purification, sacrifice, truthfulness, recitation, burnt offerings, libations, austerity, charity, forbearance, prostration, and circumambulation—[these are the means of purification]. (23)
Furthermore, other physical observances (niyamas) are recorded as vows, fasts, and the like.
[The postures are] Svastika, Gomukha, Padma, that called Haṃsa, and Brāhma. (24)
The Nṛsiṃha, Garuḍa, Kūrma, and that called Nāga are the Vaiṣṇava seats;
the Vīra, Mayūra, Vajra, and that called Siddha are the Raudra seats.
They know the Yoni-āsana as pertaining to Śakti, and the Paścimatānaka as pertaining to Śiva;
for the Nirālambana-yoga, the seat is the Nirālambana (the supportless).
Meditation is through the state of being without support; Sadāśiva is without support.
Exhalation, inhalation, and retention constitute the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇasaṃyama). || 27 ||
The withdrawal of all the sense organs from their objects is declared as *pratyāhāra* by those who know the meaning of *pratyāhāra*. (28)
The fixing of the mind upon some support is called concentration (dhāraṇā);
the contemplation of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others is declared to be meditation (dhyāna). || 29 ||
The non-fluctuation of the intellect arising from meditative absorption (dhyāna) is designated as samādhi;
however, the samādhi of no-mind (amanaska) is that which is entirely free from all thought.
When the mind has attained immobility, the vital breath becomes immobile;
for the sake of the mind's immobility, one should practice yoga together with meditation. || 31 ||
The contraction of the apāna, the restraint of the prāṇa, and the placing of the tongue upon the uvula constitute the practice of yoga. || 32 ||
When the mind has attained immobility and the vital breath has entered the central path, these signs arise individually from the conquest of the five elements. (33)
Scarcity of excrement, urine, and phlegm, health, lightness of the body, a pleasant fragrance, and a complexion like the color of gold are the first signs of yoga. (34)
Non-adherence to the tips of thorns, non-sinking in water or mud, and endurance of hunger, thirst, and so forth—this is the second characteristic of yoga. || 35 ||
Consuming abundant food and drink, endurance of heat and fire,
and seeing and hearing from a distance— this is the third characteristic of yoga.
Leaping upon the ground like a frog, leaping upon a tree like a monkey, and traveling through the sky—this is the fourth characteristic of yoga. || 37 ||

Knowledge whose object is the three periods of time, sovereignty consisting of the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, and the possession of infinite power—this is the fifth characteristic of yoga. (38)

When the vital breath has entered the *suṣumnā*, an internal sound is heard in eight ways, like the ringing of a bell, a drum, a conch, the ocean, a lute, a flute, cymbals, and other musical instruments. (39)
When the vital breath has entered the Brahma-nāḍī, which is like the sun shining through the hole of a reed, the form of the solar orb (bimba) shines forth.
As many breaths as a human being takes in a single day, so many yojanas does the sun run with every breath.
Twenty-one thousand six hundred times, day after day, this Self utters the mantra "So 'ham" for the sake of longevity. (42)
Having elided both the letter *sa* and the letter *ha*, one should apply the euphonic combination known as *pūrvarūpa*; thus, it becomes the *praṇava*. || 43 ||
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, along with the *bindu* and the *nāda*—
the wise say these are the five syllables residing within the *praṇava*.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva— all these,
together with the thirty-six principles (tattvas), abide within those syllables.
Through the grace of the Guru, one obtains yoga characterized by its eight limbs;
and through the grace of Śiva, one attains eternal perfection in yoga.
Salutation to the Guru of gurus, whose form is truth, consciousness, and bliss; who is the inner self of the *bindu* and *nāda*; and who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end. || 47 ||
Thus ends the summary of the ninth chapter in the *Mānasollāsa*, a treatise explaining the meaning of the *Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotra*.
The summary of the tenth chapter:
Since this "state of being the self of all" has been clearly elucidated in this hymn, therefore, by hearing it, reflecting upon its meaning, meditating on it, and chanting it—
Lordship, accompanied by the great power of being the self of all, would be established by itself; furthermore, that unimpeded sovereignty is transformed eightfold. || 10 ||
Having abandoned the limited sense of "I" along with its attachments, the attainment of the full sense of "I" is said to be the fruit of this hymn. || 1 ||

The prosperity of sons, grandsons, houses, fields, wealth, and grain, as well as [attainments] belonging to this world, are accomplished in the realms of heaven, the netherworld, and on earth. || 2 ||
Just as one engaged in cooking avoids cold and other such obstacles, all incidental benefits are always accomplished through this hymn of praise. (3)
For his sovereignty and lordship do not exist as something separate;
even while the Puruṣa moves, his shadow runs after him. || 4 ||
Infinite power, sovereignty, and the supernormal attainments such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest—
once one's own lordship is fully established, these indeed come about spontaneously.
He whose drops of sovereignty Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others possess,
by which they exercise their own lordship— that very Self is Sadāśiva.
Just as fragrance is experienced by one bringing a flower, even while not desiring it,
so too are all manifestations perceived by one endowed with the fullness of the sense of "I."
Aṇimā, mahimā, garimā, and likewise laghimā;
prāpti, prākāmya, īśitva, and vaśitva—these are the eight siddhis.
The entry into extremely minute living beings as their very self is the sovereignty known as *aṇimā*, belonging to the all-pervading Supreme Self. (9)

The sovereignty called "magnanimity" (mahiman) consists in the pervasive presence outside as well as within the aggregate of the thirty-six principles, beginning with the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and ending with Śiva.
The wise know "levity" (laghimā) to be the state of being like cotton in terms of lightness during the act of lifting up a body as massive as Mount Meru.
The wise know that the gravity of a teacher, equal to Mount Meru, lies in the act of extracting the limbs of one whose body consists of atoms. 12.
For a person dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), the sight of the world of Brahmā and the attainment of great sovereignty are indeed very difficult for those who lack yoga to achieve. (13)
The complete accomplishment of other perfections of attainment, such as traveling through the sky and so forth, by mere will, is designated as "irresistible will" (prākāmya). || 14 ||
Some declare that this sovereignty consists in the illumination of all objects by the light of one's own body; this is what is called "luminosity. (15)
The power of being the agent of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the worlds by mere will,
as well as the authority to direct the sun and other celestial bodies, is designated as "lordship" (īśitva).
All the worlds, together with their guardians, are under the control of those Śiva-yogins; thus, that sovereignty known as "mastery" (vaśitva) is easily attained by them. 17.
The gods remain under the control of that brahmin who knows this;
how much more so, then, kings, tigers, serpents, women, men, and the like? (18)
For those whose minds are uninterrupted by the sovereignty over all forms of existence and whose meditative concentrations are fully ripened, what indeed is there that cannot be accomplished? (19)
The wise person should recite this hymn and contemplate the state of being the Self of all,
having abandoned desire for inferior fruits such as rebirth in heaven and the like.
The wise man does not consider sovereignty over heaven and the like to be true empire;
for him, that alone is empire which is self-sovereignty within the Self.
All supernatural powers attend upon one who possesses every form of self-cultivation;
therefore, with a disciplined mind, one should exercise sovereign mastery over the self. (22)
For that high-souled one who has supreme devotion to the Divine, and to the Guru as to the Divine, these truths thus explained indeed shine forth. 23.
May this Light, who by means of his power consisting of luminosity is the maker of light for all lights, and who illumines the entire universe, shine forth. 24.
Thus ends the summary of the tenth chapter in the *Mānasollāsa*, a composition that elucidates the meaning of the *Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotra*.
Thus ends the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotrabhāvārthavārtika*, composed by the venerable teacher Sureśvarācārya, based on the work of the illustrious teacher Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda.
Oṃ tat sat.
